hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: A nearby-business search using geohash queries the user's cell plus its 8 neighbouring cells. Why the neighbours?
options: Geohash cells are circles, so neighbours fill the gaps between them
A point just across a cell boundary can be very close yet have a completely different geohash prefix
Neighbouring cells hold older versions of the same businesses
Geohash ignores longitude, so neighbours are needed to cover east-west distance
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: Shared prefixes imply closeness, but closeness doesn't imply a shared prefix: two points a metre apart on opposite sides of a boundary can differ from the first character. Checking the 8 neighbours covers that edge case.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: For a 'businesses within ~500 m' search, which geohash precision is a typical choice for the search cells?
options: Length 4 (about 39 km x 20 km)
Length 5 (about 4.9 km x 4.9 km)
Length 6 (about 1.2 km x 0.6 km)
Length 8 (about 38 m x 19 m)
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: A length-6 cell plus its neighbours comfortably covers a 500 m radius without scanning a huge area. Length 8 cells are so small that you would need to query hundreds of cells to cover 500 m.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: Why might you choose a quadtree over a fixed grid to index millions of businesses?
options: It adapts to density: dense areas are subdivided further so each leaf holds a bounded number of places
It offers O(1) lookup for any radius query
It handles constantly moving points with no rebalancing cost
It is natively supported as a Redis data type
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: A fixed grid gives Manhattan and a desert the same cell size, so some cells are overloaded and others empty. A quadtree splits only where density is high. Updates for moving points are actually a weakness of quadtrees.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: A nearby-friends feature has 10 million concurrent users, each sending a location update every 30 seconds. Roughly how many location updates per second must the system ingest?
options: About 33,000
About 3.3 million
About 10 million
About 334,000
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: 10,000,000 / 30 is about 333,000 updates per second. Each update may fan out to several online friends, so outbound messages are a multiple of this.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: Which architecture fits a nearby-friends feature where friends within 5 miles see each other's location update in near real time?
options: Store locations in PostgreSQL and have each client poll for friends' locations every second
On every update, run a geospatial radius query over all users and push to everyone found
Persistent WebSocket connections plus a pub/sub channel per user; friends subscribe to each other's channels and the server forwards an update only if the distance is within range
Broadcast every update to every connection on the same WebSocket server
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: Pub/sub per user limits fan-out to actual friends, and the distance check on receipt filters out far-away friends. A global radius query on every update finds strangers rather than friends and is far more expensive.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: How does Redis store points added with GEOADD?
options: In an R-tree maintained by a built-in geospatial module
In a sorted set whose score is a 52-bit interleaved geohash value
In a hash of member to latitude/longitude string
In a quadtree that is rebuilt on every insert
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: Redis GEO commands are built on sorted sets: coordinates are encoded as a 52-bit geohash used as the score, and radius searches become score-range scans over neighbouring cells. There is no R-tree.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: Why is an in-memory quadtree built at startup a good fit for business locations but a poor fit for user locations that change every few seconds?
options: Quadtrees can hold at most four points per node, which users exceed
Quadtrees store data on disk, which is too slow for users
Quadtrees cannot answer radius queries, only exact matches
Frequent moves mean constant removals, reinsertions and node splits/merges, while businesses barely change
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: Businesses change rarely, so building the tree once and refreshing it occasionally is cheap. Moving users would force constant restructuring; a geohash key in a cache with TTL is cheaper for them. Quadtrees do support range and radius queries.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: Which statements about geohash are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It is a base32 string where each character adds 5 bits of precision
A longer shared prefix means both points fall within a smaller common cell
All cells of the same length cover the same ground area anywhere on Earth
Any two nearby points always share a long common prefix
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: Each base32 character encodes 5 bits, and longer prefixes mean smaller cells. Cells are equal in degrees, not in ground area, which varies with latitude. Nearby points across a boundary may share no prefix at all.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: You use Redis pub/sub as the message bus for nearby friends. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Messages are not persisted; a subscriber that is offline misses them, which is acceptable for ephemeral locations
Channels can be spread across a fleet of pub/sub servers by consistently hashing the user id
Every message is written to a durable log so late-joining subscribers can replay it
In Redis Cluster, classic PUBLISH is broadcast to all nodes, while sharded pub/sub (SPUBLISH, Redis 7) routes by channel hash slot
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget, which suits locations that are stale in seconds anyway. Sharded pub/sub in Redis 7 avoids cluster-wide broadcast. Durable replay is what Redis Streams or Kafka provide, not pub/sub.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: A geohash of length 8 represents a smaller area than a geohash of length 5.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: Each extra character adds 5 bits, splitting the cell into 32 sub-cells. Length 8 is about 38 m x 19 m; length 5 is about 4.9 km x 4.9 km.

hld-vol2-specialized:0.prompt: Searching only the single geohash cell that contains the user is enough to guarantee finding the nearest business.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:0.explanation: The nearest business may sit just across a cell boundary, closer than anything inside the user's own cell. You must also search neighbours and expand when results are too few.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: Why do map services serve the map as tiles at discrete zoom levels?
options: The client downloads only tiles for the current viewport and zoom, and static tiles cache well on a CDN
Mobile devices cannot render vector graphics, so tiles are required
Tiles make shortest-path routing faster
Tiles are needed for the device's GPS to work
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: Tiling splits the world into small, cacheable, URL-addressable pieces, so panning and zooming only fetch what is visible, mostly from a CDN. Routing and GPS are separate concerns.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: In the standard web-map tiling scheme, zoom level z has 2^z x 2^z tiles. About how many tiles exist at zoom level 10?
options: About 1,000
About 20,000
About 1.05 million
About 1.07 billion
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: 2^10 x 2^10 = 4^10 = 1,048,576 tiles. Tile counts grow 4x per zoom level, which is why the deepest levels dominate storage and are often rendered on demand.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: What is a main advantage of vector tiles over raster (PNG) tiles?
options: They don't need the client's GPU or any rendering on the device
They usually have smaller payloads and allow client-side styling, rotation and smooth zoom
They cannot be cached by CDNs, which keeps data fresh
They are better for satellite imagery
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: Vector tiles carry geometry, which the client renders, so one tile set supports many styles, languages and smooth zooming. Satellite imagery is inherently raster, and vector tiles cache on CDNs just as well.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: Plain Dijkstra on a continent-sized road graph is too slow per query. What do production routing engines typically do?
options: Use breadth-first search, which is faster on road networks
Precompute all-pairs shortest paths nightly with Floyd-Warshall
Use Bellman-Ford, which handles more road types
Use preprocessing-based speedups such as contraction hierarchies or hierarchical partitioning so each query explores few nodes
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: Contraction hierarchies and partition-based methods preprocess the graph so queries take milliseconds. Floyd-Warshall is O(n^3) time and O(n^2) storage, which is infeasible for hundreds of millions of nodes; BFS ignores edge weights.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: A* for travel-time routing uses 'straight-line distance divided by the maximum speed limit' as its heuristic. Why must the heuristic never overestimate the remaining cost?
options: An admissible heuristic guarantees A* still returns an optimal path
Overestimating makes the heuristic slower to compute
Overestimating causes A* to visit every node in the graph
A* only works with heuristics measured in meters
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: If the heuristic never overestimates, A* cannot finalize a suboptimal path before the optimal one. An overestimating heuristic may find routes faster but can return a non-optimal route.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: ETAs must reflect current traffic, but the routing engine relies on heavy preprocessing. How is live traffic usually incorporated?
options: Rebuild the full contraction hierarchy from scratch for every request
Use static road distances and add a fixed traffic buffer to every ETA
Use a technique whose edge weights can be updated separately from preprocessing (e.g. customizable route planning) and refresh travel times from live probe data
Ask users to report traffic and only reroute when reports arrive
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: Customizable approaches split the expensive metric-independent preprocessing from a fast customization step, so edge travel times from GPS probes can be refreshed every few minutes. Rebuilding per request is far too slow.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: GPS points from phones are noisy and drift off roads. What is the process of snapping a trace to the most likely sequence of road segments called?
options: Geocoding
Map matching
Reverse geocoding
Tile rendering
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: Map matching (often done with a Hidden Markov Model) aligns noisy GPS traces to the road network, which is needed for both navigation and building traffic speeds. Geocoding converts addresses to coordinates.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: Which design choices are reasonable for a navigation service? Select all that apply.
options: Serve map tiles from a CDN
Partition the road graph into routing tiles that servers load on demand
Run Floyd-Warshall nightly to precompute every possible route
Batch location updates on the client to save battery and bandwidth
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: CDN tiles, partitioned routing graphs and batched client updates are standard. All-pairs precomputation is infeasible at road-network scale in both time and storage.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: Which statements about rerouting and ETA during active navigation are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Detect off-route driving by comparing the map-matched position with the planned route
Suggest a new route when traffic makes an alternative faster by more than a threshold
Recompute every active user's route every second regardless of conditions
Combine live and historical speeds because live probe data is sparse on minor roads
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: Rerouting is event-driven (off-route, significant traffic change), and ETAs blend historical patterns with live data. Recomputing every route every second wastes huge compute for almost no benefit.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: Geocoding converts a street address into latitude and longitude coordinates.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: Geocoding is address to coordinates; reverse geocoding is coordinates to a human-readable address.

hld-vol2-specialized:1.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm returns correct shortest paths even when some edge weights are negative.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:1.explanation: Dijkstra assumes a finalized node can't later get a shorter path, which breaks with negative weights. Bellman-Ford handles negative edges. Road travel times are non-negative, so Dijkstra-based methods work for routing.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: What ordering guarantee does Apache Kafka provide?
options: Total order across all partitions of a topic
Order only within a single partition
Order across all topics of the cluster
No ordering guarantee at all
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: Kafka orders records within a partition by offset. Across partitions there is no global order, which is why related events must share a key to land on the same partition.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group has 10 consumers. How many consumers actively receive messages?
options: 10, each partition is split across consumers
1, a single leader consumer reads everything
5, Kafka uses half of the consumers as standbys
6, and the other 4 sit idle
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: Within a group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so parallelism is capped by the partition count. The 4 extra consumers are idle until a rebalance gives them a partition.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: Events for each order must be processed in sequence. How should the producer publish them?
options: Use order_id as the message key so all events for an order go to the same partition
Use round-robin partitioning to balance load evenly
Create one partition per consumer and choose partitions randomly
Put the event timestamp in the key so consumers can sort events
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: The default partitioner hashes the key, so the same order_id always lands on the same partition, which is consumed in order. Round-robin spreads one order's events across partitions and loses ordering.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: A consumer commits its offset right after polling, before processing, and then crashes mid-processing. Which delivery semantics does this give?
options: At-least-once: the message is redelivered after restart
Exactly-once: the commit and processing are atomic
At-most-once: the uncommitted work is lost because the offset already moved past it
It depends only on the producer's acks setting
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: Committing before processing means a crash skips the message on restart, so it is processed at most once. Committing after processing flips this to at-least-once with possible duplicates.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: What does Kafka's idempotent producer combined with transactions actually provide?
options: End-to-end exactly-once for any external database without extra work
Atomic read-process-write across Kafka topics and consumer offsets; side effects outside Kafka still need their own idempotency
Global ordering across all partitions of a topic
No duplicates even when consumers auto-commit and write to an external DB
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: Kafka transactions make output records and offset commits atomic within Kafka. Calling an API or writing to Postgres is outside that transaction, so those sinks need idempotency keys or a transactional outbox/inbox.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: A topic has replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, and the producer uses acks=all. Two of the three replicas go down. What happens to writes?
options: They are written to the leader only and replicated later
They are buffered by the broker until replicas return
The producer automatically falls back to acks=1
They are rejected with a not-enough-replicas error, trading availability for durability
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: With only one in-sync replica, acks=all cannot be satisfied under min.insync.replicas=2, so the broker rejects writes. This configuration deliberately refuses writes rather than risk losing acknowledged data.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: Kafka keeps messages after they are consumed until retention expires. What does this enable compared with a classic queue that deletes on acknowledgement?
options: Multiple independent consumer groups and replay by resetting offsets
Strict global ordering of all messages
Lower latency than any in-memory queue
Automatic exactly-once delivery to every consumer
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: Because the log is retained, each consumer group tracks its own offset, and you can rewind to reprocess. Retention has nothing to do with global ordering or exactly-once delivery.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: Which events trigger a consumer group rebalance in Kafka? Select all that apply.
options: A new consumer joins the group
A consumer exceeds max.poll.interval.ms between polls
Partitions are added to a subscribed topic
A producer sends a message with a key never seen before
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: Membership changes (join, leave, being considered dead after a slow poll) and partition count changes trigger reassignment. New keys just hash to existing partitions and don't affect the group.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: One message always fails processing and blocks its partition. Which handling strategies are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Retry a bounded number of times, then publish it to a dead-letter topic and move on
Silently commit past it without recording it anywhere
Route it through retry topics with increasing delays before the DLQ
Add partitions to the topic so the blocked message moves elsewhere
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: Bounded retries plus delayed retry topics and a DLQ keep the partition moving while preserving the message for investigation. Silently skipping loses data; adding partitions doesn't move existing messages.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: Adding partitions to an existing Kafka topic can change which partition a given key maps to, so new and old messages for that key may be on different partitions.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: The default partitioner uses hash(key) mod partitionCount, so changing the count remaps keys. Existing data stays where it was, which can break per-key ordering around the change.

hld-vol2-specialized:2.prompt: Within one consumer group, two consumers can read the same partition at the same time to double throughput.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:2.explanation: A partition is assigned to only one consumer per group. To get more parallelism you need more partitions, or a separate consumer group, which receives every message independently.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: Which observability signal best answers 'why was this particular request slow as it passed through five services'?
options: Aggregated metrics such as request rate and p99 latency
Uptime checks from external probes
A distributed trace showing spans for each service hop
Host-level CPU and memory dashboards
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: A trace follows one request across services with timing per span, pinpointing where the time went. Metrics are aggregated, so they show that latency rose but not which hop caused it for a given request.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: Why put Kafka between metric collectors and the time-series storage writers?
options: Kafka compresses metrics better than any TSDB
It buffers bursts and decouples the two sides, so writers can fall behind and catch up without dropping data
It removes the need for a time-series database
It makes alert evaluation exactly-once
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: A durable buffer absorbs ingest spikes and storage outages, and lets other consumers (anomaly detection, archiving) read the same stream. You still need a TSDB for efficient queries.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: An alert fires whenever CPU exceeds 90%, including 20-second spikes, and pages on-call several times a night. What is the best first fix?
options: Lower the threshold to 80% so issues are caught earlier
Raise the scrape interval so short spikes are not recorded
Send the alert by email instead of paging
Require the condition to hold for a duration (e.g. 'for: 5m') before firing
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: A pending duration filters transient spikes while still catching sustained problems. Coarser scraping only hides data, and switching channels leaves a noisy, non-actionable alert in place.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. A simple 'error rate above 0.1% for 5 minutes' alert is noisy for blips yet slow for a full outage. What is the recommended improvement?
options: Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts, e.g. page when both the 1-hour and 5-minute windows burn the budget at 14.4x
A single 30-day error-budget alert that fires when the budget hits zero
Alert on CPU instead of errors, since it leads errors
Increase the threshold to 1% errors over 1 hour
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: Burn-rate alerts measure how fast the error budget is being spent; 14.4x over an hour consumes 2% of a 30-day budget, and the short window confirms it is still happening. A budget-exhausted alert fires far too late.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: A network partition causes 500 hosts to fire the same alert simultaneously. Which Alertmanager feature turns this into one notification?
options: Silences created after the page arrives
A longer rule evaluation interval
Grouping alerts by labels such as alertname and cluster
Deduplicating alerts by host name
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: Grouping batches alerts sharing chosen labels into a single notification (inhibition can additionally suppress dependent alerts). Deduplicating by host keeps 500 distinct alerts because each host is different.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: Head-based sampling at 1% means rare error traces are usually dropped. What is the main alternative and its cost?
options: Sample 100% of traces at the client, which costs nothing extra
Tail-based sampling in the collector, keeping all error or slow traces, at the cost of buffering every span until each trace completes
Sample by service name so each service keeps 1%
Convert traces into logs, which are always cheaper to store
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: Tail sampling decides after seeing the whole trace, so it can keep interesting ones, but collectors must hold spans in memory and route all spans of a trace to the same instance. Per-service 1% sampling still drops most errors.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: Why does a TSDB such as Prometheus append incoming samples to a write-ahead log before adding them to its in-memory head block?
options: So in-memory data that hasn't been flushed to disk blocks can be recovered after a crash
So queries read from the WAL instead of memory
Because compression only works on WAL files
So remote clients can tail the WAL for alerts
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: Recent samples live in memory for hours before being compacted into blocks; the WAL lets the server replay them after a restart. Queries are served from the head block and persisted blocks, not the WAL.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: Which are good alerting practices? Select all that apply.
options: Alert on user-facing symptoms such as error rate and latency rather than every possible cause
Make every page actionable and link it to a runbook
Page on-call for every warning-level threshold on every metric
Route by severity: urgent issues page, lower-severity ones create tickets
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: Symptom-based, actionable, severity-routed alerts keep pages meaningful. Paging on every warning causes alert fatigue, and people start ignoring pages.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: How do horizontally scaled metrics backends (Thanos, Cortex, Mimir style) handle storage at scale? Select all that apply.
options: Upload compacted blocks to object storage for long-term retention
Shard ingesters by a hash of the series labels, with replication
Queriers fan out to stores, merge results and deduplicate HA replicas
Keep all data forever on a single large node's local SSD
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: These systems use hash-sharded, replicated ingesters, cheap object storage for history, and fan-out queriers that merge and deduplicate. A single node caps both capacity and availability.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: Logs and traces can be correlated by writing the trace ID into each log line.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: Putting the trace ID (and span ID) into structured logs lets you jump from a slow trace to its logs and back. OpenTelemetry log correlation is built on this.

hld-vol2-specialized:3.prompt: In Prometheus, if a metric stops being reported and its series disappears, an alert like 'errors > 0' automatically fires because the missing value is treated as zero.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:3.explanation: A missing series yields no result, so a threshold rule simply stops matching; it is not treated as zero and it does not fire. Use absent() or up == 0 alerts to detect disappeared targets.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: Which protocol do mail servers use to transfer email to each other?
options: IMAP
POP3
SMTP
JMAP
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: SMTP handles server-to-server relay (and client submission). IMAP, POP3 and JMAP are protocols for clients to read mail from their own mailbox.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: How does a sending mail server find where to deliver mail addressed to someone@example.com?
options: It looks up the MX records for example.com and tries the lowest preference value first
It looks up the A record for mail.example.com by convention
It asks the recipient's IMAP server for a delivery address
It looks up the TXT record containing the SPF policy
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: MX records list the domain's mail exchangers with preference values; lower is tried first. SPF in TXT records authorizes senders and says nothing about where to deliver.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: Which mechanism adds a cryptographic signature over selected headers and the body so the receiver can verify the message came from the signing domain and wasn't altered?
options: SPF
DMARC
STARTTLS
DKIM
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: DKIM signs the message with the domain's private key; receivers verify with the public key in DNS. SPF only checks whether the sending IP is authorized, and DMARC is a policy built on top of SPF and DKIM.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: A user reads mail on a phone and a laptop and wants folders and read/unread status to stay in sync. Which client access protocol fits?
options: POP3, because it downloads messages to each device
IMAP, because state such as folders and flags lives on the server
SMTP, because it pushes changes to every device
FTP, because mailboxes are stored as files
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: IMAP keeps the mailbox and its flags on the server, so every client sees the same state. POP3 is designed to download (often delete) messages, so state diverges between devices.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: You must store email for a billion users. Typical queries list a folder sorted by date and show unread counts; bodies and attachments are large. Which storage design fits best?
options: One relational database holding all messages, with bodies and attachments as BLOBs
Elasticsearch as the single primary store for metadata and bodies
Metadata in a store partitioned by user_id and clustered by folder and time, with bodies and attachments in object storage
One file per user on local disk on the server that received the mail
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: Partitioning by user keeps each mailbox's queries on one shard, and clustering by folder/time makes listings range scans. Large immutable blobs belong in object storage. A single relational DB can't scale to that volume, and local files lack durability.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: Why is mailbox full-text search usually built as per-user partitioned indexes rather than one global index sorted for relevance?
options: A global index ranks results better, but per-user indexes are cheaper to license
Search libraries cannot hold more than a million documents in one index
A global index is cheaper to update when each new email arrives
Every query is scoped to one user, so partitioning by user keeps searches on one shard and isolates users from each other
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: Users only search their own mail, so a per-user partition means a query touches one small shard and a heavy user can't slow others. A global index would make every write and query hit a huge shared structure.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: How should an inbound spam-filtering pipeline be ordered?
options: Run cheap checks first (IP reputation, blocklists, SPF/DKIM/DMARC results), then content-based ML classification on what remains
Run the expensive ML classifier on every message before any other check
Deliver every message first and scan the inbox later in a batch job
Rely only on users clicking 'report spam'
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: Cheap connection-level checks reject a large share of spam before costly content analysis, saving compute. Delivering first exposes users to phishing and makes cleanup harder.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: Which practices improve outbound deliverability for a new email-sending service? Select all that apply.
options: Publish SPF, DKIM and a DMARC policy for the sending domain
Warm up new sending IPs by gradually increasing volume
Process bounces and complaints and suppress those addresses
Rotate through many random sending domains to stay ahead of filters
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: Authentication, IP warm-up and list hygiene build sender reputation. Rotating random domains looks like spammer behaviour (snowshoeing) and damages deliverability.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: Which statements about SMTP delivery are correct? Select all that apply.
options: On a 4xx temporary failure, the sender retries with backoff, often for days
On a 5xx permanent failure, the sender stops and returns a bounce (DSN) to the original sender
A receiving server should reply 250 only after the message is durably stored, since that transfers responsibility
SMTP guarantees end-to-end encryption from the sender's device to the recipient's device
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: SMTP is store-and-forward: a 250 means the receiver has taken responsibility, 4xx means try again later, 5xx means give up and bounce. STARTTLS encrypts individual hops only, not end to end.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: DMARC lets a domain owner tell receivers what to do (none, quarantine or reject) with mail that fails SPF/DKIM alignment, and where to send reports.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: DMARC publishes a policy (p=none/quarantine/reject) and reporting addresses in DNS, based on whether SPF or DKIM pass and align with the From domain.

hld-vol2-specialized:4.prompt: Deduplicating attachments by content hash is never useful in email storage, because every message is unique.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:4.explanation: Messages are unique, but attachments often aren't: the same file sent to 200 recipients or forwarded repeatedly can be stored once and referenced by its hash, saving a lot of storage.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: Why do S3-style object stores separate the metadata service from the data storage nodes?
options: Metadata must be stored on tape for durability
Metadata is small and needs fast consistent lookups and listings, while data is large immutable blobs, so each side scales independently
Data nodes cannot store keys longer than 64 bytes
Separation removes the need for any replication
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: Name lookups and listings have very different access patterns from streaming gigabytes of bytes. Splitting them lets the metadata tier optimize for consistency and the data tier for throughput and cheap capacity.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: An object store uses Reed-Solomon erasure coding with 8 data fragments and 4 parity fragments. What are the storage overhead and failure tolerance?
options: 1.5x overhead; any 2 fragments can be lost
3x overhead; any 4 fragments can be lost
1.33x overhead; any 4 fragments can be lost
1.5x overhead; any 4 fragments can be lost
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: 12 fragments store 8 fragments' worth of data: 12 / 8 = 1.5x. Any 8 of the 12 can rebuild the object, so up to 4 can be lost. 3x replication tolerates only 2 losses at double the cost.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: What is the main trade-off of erasure coding compared with 3x replication?
options: Much lower storage cost, but more CPU and network for encoding, degraded reads and repairs
Higher durability with higher storage cost
Faster small reads because fragments are read in parallel from one disk
No trade-off; erasure coding is strictly better
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: Erasure coding cuts overhead (e.g. 1.5x versus 3x), but reconstruction must read from many nodes and compute parity. That is why hot or small data is often replicated and cold data erasure-coded.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: All 12 fragments of an RS(8,4) object were placed on servers in the same rack. What is the main risk?
options: Reads are slower because fragments share one network switch
Parity fragments cannot be computed within a single rack
One rack-level failure (power, top-of-rack switch) removes more than 4 fragments at once, making the object unavailable or lost
No risk, since erasure coding already tolerates 4 failures
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: The 4-failure tolerance assumes independent failures. Correlated failures within a rack or AZ break that assumption, so fragments must be spread across failure domains.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: Why do object stores often pack many small objects into large data files instead of storing one file per object?
options: Small files cannot be erasure-coded at all
Per-file filesystem overhead (inodes, metadata, seeks) is huge for billions of tiny objects; appending to large files and recording (file, offset, size) is far cheaper
Packing makes each object mutable in place
Large files encrypt faster than small ones
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: Billions of tiny files exhaust inodes and make metadata operations dominate. Appending to large files turns writes into sequential I/O; the metadata service maps each object to its location.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: An object is deleted: its metadata is marked deleted, but its bytes remain inside a large packed data file. How is the space usually reclaimed?
options: The bytes are zeroed in place immediately
They are never reclaimed; storage just grows
The filesystem's TRIM command frees them automatically
Background compaction copies live objects into new files, updates metadata, then deletes the old files
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: Compaction (garbage collection) rewrites files that contain mostly dead data, preserving immutability of written files. Zeroing bytes in place wouldn't free space in the file anyway.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: A client must upload a 5 GB file over an unreliable connection. Which object-storage feature is designed for this?
options: Multipart upload: parts are uploaded in parallel, retried individually, then combined with a completion call
Increasing the HTTP timeout for one big PUT
Splitting the file into separate objects that the client must reassemble on every read
Uploading through a byte-range PATCH on the existing object
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: Multipart upload lets a failed part be retried without restarting, and the parts become one object on completion. Incomplete uploads still use storage, so lifecycle rules should clean them up.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: Which techniques do object stores use to reach very high durability? Select all that apply.
options: Checksums on write and periodic background scrubbing to detect silent corruption
Replicating or erasure-coding data across multiple availability zones
Repairing corrupted or lost fragments from replicas or parity
Relying only on local RAID inside each storage node
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: Durability comes from detecting corruption, spreading redundancy across independent failure domains, and repairing quickly. Node-level RAID doesn't survive losing the whole node, rack or AZ.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: Which statements about the metadata service for prefix-based LIST operations are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Storing keys sorted in range partitions makes a prefix LIST a range scan
Hash-partitioning by full key forces prefix listings to query every shard
Metadata should be stored inside the data blobs so no separate index is needed
Hot key prefixes may require splitting range partitions to spread load
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: Range partitioning preserves key order for listing but can create hot ranges that must be split; hash partitioning spreads load but scatters prefixes. Without a separate index, listing would require scanning all data.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: Amazon S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for new objects, overwrites and LIST operations.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: Since December 2020, S3 is strongly consistent for GET, PUT and LIST, so a successful write is immediately visible. Earlier it was eventually consistent for overwrites and listings.

hld-vol2-specialized:5.prompt: With erasure coding, reading an object when one data fragment is missing costs no more than reading a healthy object.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:5.explanation: A degraded read must fetch parity fragments from other nodes and decode the missing data, which adds network, CPU and latency. That is part of erasure coding's trade-off.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: In a double-entry ledger, what invariant does every transaction satisfy?
options: Each transaction touches exactly one account
The receiving account's balance is always updated first
Total debits equal total credits, so the entries sum to zero
Each entry stores the account's running balance instead of an amount
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: Money moves between accounts, so every transaction has balancing debit and credit entries. That makes errors detectable: if the ledger doesn't sum to zero, something is wrong.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: In a Node.js wallet backed by PostgreSQL, how should monetary amounts be represented?
options: JavaScript numbers, rounded with toFixed(2) before saving
Integer minor units (e.g. cents as bigint/BigInt) or NUMERIC, always with a currency code
A float8 column, since it has 15 digits of precision
Strings converted with parseFloat when doing arithmetic
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: Binary floating point can't represent values like 0.1 exactly, so sums drift (0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3). Integer minor units or decimal types are exact. parseFloat brings back the same float problem.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: A client's POST /transfers times out and the client retries. How do you prevent the transfer from happening twice?
options: Rate-limit the client to one request per second
Reject any transfer with the same amount within 10 seconds
Rely on TCP retransmission to avoid duplicates
Have the client send an idempotency key stored under a unique constraint; on a repeat, return the stored result
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: The server records the key with the outcome in the same transaction as the transfer, so a retry returns the original result. Amount-based heuristics block legitimate identical transfers and miss real duplicates.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: In PostgreSQL, two concurrent withdrawals each read balance = 100, check it is at least 100, then write balance - 100. The balance ends up at -100. Which fix is correct?
options: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = $1 AND balance >= 100, and treat 0 updated rows as insufficient funds
Keep READ COMMITTED with SELECT then UPDATE, but add a retry loop
Wrap the check in an in-process mutex in the Node service
Read the balance from a replica so the check is cheaper
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: The conditional update makes the check and debit one atomic statement (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE also works). An in-process mutex doesn't help when several Node instances run, and a retry loop doesn't fix the race.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: Accounts A and B live on different database shards, and you want to avoid two-phase commit. What is a common way to transfer money between them?
options: Two independent writes with no tracking, since failures are rare
A global lock over all shards during every transfer
A saga: debit A into a pending state, credit B, compensate A on failure, with every step idempotent and tracked
A nightly batch job that fixes any mismatched balances
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: A saga breaks the transfer into idempotent local steps with compensations and a recorded state machine, so it can resume or undo after failures. Untracked writes can lose or create money when one side fails.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: An event-sourced wallet derives balances by replaying all events. Reads are getting slow for old, busy accounts. What is the standard fix?
options: Delete old events once they are older than a year
Store periodic snapshots and/or maintain a read-model projection, replaying only events after the snapshot
Switch reads to a cache with a 24-hour TTL
Merge old events into one event and rewrite history
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: Snapshots and projections keep the event log as the source of truth while making reads cheap. Deleting or rewriting events destroys the audit trail, which is the main reason to use event sourcing.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: A credit of $50 was posted to the wrong account. How should it be corrected in a ledger?
options: Post a reversing entry, then post the correct entry
Update the original entry's account id in place
Delete the original entry and insert the correct one
Adjust the account's cached balance without touching the ledger
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: Ledgers are append-only: corrections are new entries, so the history shows what happened and when. Editing or deleting entries breaks auditability and reconciliation.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: Which statements about event sourcing for a wallet are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It provides a complete audit trail of every change
Current state can be rebuilt by replaying events
Evolving the schema of old events needs versioning or upcasting
Querying current state needs no extra components
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: Event sourcing gives auditability and replay, but stored events live forever, so schema changes need versioning. Queries on current state usually need projections or snapshots, which are extra components.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: Which statements about ledger reconciliation are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Compare the internal ledger daily with bank or payment-provider settlement reports
The sum of all ledger entries per currency should be zero
Reconciliation is unnecessary when double-entry bookkeeping is used
Mismatches go to an investigation queue and are fixed with adjusting entries
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: Double-entry keeps the ledger internally consistent but can't detect disagreement with external systems (missed webhooks, fees, chargebacks). Reconciliation catches those, and fixes are new entries.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: Storing money as IEEE-754 floating point is fine as long as you round to two decimals when displaying it.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: Rounding only hides the error in display; stored sums still accumulate representation error, and comparisons such as balance >= amount can be wrong. Use integer minor units or decimals.

hld-vol2-specialized:6.prompt: An idempotency key should be stored with a hash of the request, so a reused key with a different payload can be rejected.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:6.explanation: If a client mistakenly reuses a key for a different transfer, returning the old result would silently drop the new request. Comparing request hashes lets the server return a clear error instead.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: In an exchange order book, what does price-time priority mean?
options: Larger orders match first, then earlier ones
Orders are matched randomly among the best prices
The best price matches first, and among orders at the same price the earliest one matches first
Market makers always match before other participants
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: Price-time (FIFO) priority rewards the best price first and then whoever arrived first at that price. Size-based (pro-rata) matching exists in some markets but isn't price-time priority.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: The ask side has 300 shares at 100.10 and 500 shares at 100.20. A market buy order for 600 shares arrives. What is the average fill price?
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: It fills 300 at 100.10 (30,030) and 300 at 100.20 (30,060): 60,090 / 600 = 100.15. 100.16 is what you get by wrongly weighting by the full 500 shares at 100.20.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: Bids: 400 @ 99.95, 300 @ 99.90, 500 @ 99.85. A limit sell for 1,000 @ 99.90 arrives. What happens?
options: Fills 1,000 at 99.90
Fills 400 @ 99.95 and 300 @ 99.90; the remaining 300 rests on the book as an ask at 99.90
Rests entirely as an ask at 99.90 because it is a limit order
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: A sell limit at 99.90 matches any bid at or above 99.90, best price first. The 99.85 bid is below the limit, so the remaining 300 shares rest on the book at 99.90.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: Why do exchanges typically run a single-threaded matching engine per instrument behind a sequencer?
options: Multithreading is impossible in the languages exchanges use
Regulators forbid multiple threads in trading systems
It minimizes memory usage per instrument
Processing a totally ordered input stream deterministically means replaying the same log yields identical state, enabling recovery and hot standbys
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: Determinism plus a sequenced input log means any replica fed the same sequence produces the same book and fills, which gives fast failover and auditability. A single thread on in-memory data is also extremely fast because it avoids locks.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: The primary matching engine fails. How does a backup take over without losing or duplicating fills?
options: The backup consumes the same sequenced input and processes it deterministically; it resumes from the last sequence number, and outputs are deduplicated by sequence number
The backup reloads the order book from a database snapshot taken nightly
Participants resubmit all their open orders after the failover
The backup re-matches all of today's orders from scratch and re-sends every fill
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: Feeding the hot standby the same sequenced log keeps it in lockstep, and sequence numbers let downstream systems drop duplicates. A nightly snapshot would lose the whole day's state.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: Which data structure supports an order book with fast best-price access and O(1) add/cancel at a known price level?
options: One sorted array of all orders
A binary heap of orders only
Price levels each holding a doubly linked FIFO list, an order_id to node map, and a sorted structure (or array) of price levels
A hash map from order_id to order, with nothing else
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: The linked list keeps time priority within a level, the hash map finds an order for O(1) cancel, and the sorted levels give the best price. A heap makes cancellations O(n); a sorted array makes insertion O(n).

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: Why do exchanges often publish market data using UDP multicast?
options: UDP guarantees delivery, unlike TCP
It fans out to many participants with low, uniform latency; receivers detect gaps by sequence number and request retransmission
Multicast encrypts data automatically
It lets each participant receive a personalized feed
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: Multicast sends one packet to all subscribers at once, which is fast and fair. UDP doesn't guarantee delivery, so feeds carry sequence numbers and offer recovery or retransmission channels.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: Which are appropriate pre-trade risk checks? Select all that apply.
options: Check buying power and position limits before the order enters the book
Price collars and fat-finger checks against a reference price
Run risk checks asynchronously after matching to keep latency low
Reject orders above a maximum quantity or notional value
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: Pre-trade checks must run before matching, or a bad order can execute before anyone notices. Checking after matching is post-trade surveillance, which can't undo the fill.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: Which techniques do low-latency matching engines commonly use? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the entire order book in memory
Avoid allocations and GC pauses in the hot path, e.g. with object pools
Write every order synchronously to a relational database before matching
Use a ring buffer and an append-only event log, as in the LMAX Disruptor
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: In-memory books, allocation-free hot paths and ring buffers with sequential journaling keep latency in microseconds. A synchronous relational write per order adds milliseconds; durability comes from the sequenced log instead.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: A market order guarantees the execution price but not that the order will execute.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: It is the reverse: a market order executes immediately against available liquidity at whatever prices are there, so the price isn't guaranteed. A limit order guarantees the price (or better) but not execution.

hld-vol2-specialized:7.prompt: Under price-time priority, many exchanges let an order keep its time priority when its quantity is reduced, but it loses priority when the quantity is increased.
options: True
False
hld-vol2-specialized:7.explanation: Reducing quantity doesn't disadvantage others queued behind, so priority is kept; increasing it would let a trader jump the queue with new size, so it is treated as a new order at the back of the level.
